lines.text: You just saw a game.
But here's the interesting question...
How do you actually make something like this?
Do you open your computer, and immediately start writing code?
No.
You start by thinking.
Good creators start by understanding the thing they're going to build.
A finished product can look complicated.
But creators learn to break complicated things into smaller pieces.
The player. The world. Obstacles. Controls. The score. The rules. Game over. And restart.
Eight pieces. That's all this game really is.
Now, let's step away from the computer completely.
Before we build it digitally, we're going to design it on paper.
Here's the game area. The ground. Our dinosaur. An obstacle. And the score.
Then we add what things do. The dinosaur jumps. The obstacle moves toward the player. The score goes up while you survive. And if they collide... game over.
Plus a button, so the player can restart.
It doesn't have to be beautiful. Look at this dinosaur. It's basically a potato with legs.
That's fine. The point isn't art. The point is to make the idea visible.
When you put your idea on paper, you can see it.
You can change it.
You can spot what's missing.
And you can explain it to somebody else.
This is how all your development and product building should start.
Don't start by building.
Start by understanding what you're building.
Websites. Apps. Games. Businesses. Creative projects. They all start right here.
Now let's ask our design some questions.
What are we making?
A Dino Runner game.
Who is using it?
The player.
What can the player do?
Jump, and avoid obstacles.
What happens in the game?
Obstacles move toward the player.
How does the player know they're doing well?
The score goes up.
What happens when the dinosaur hits an obstacle?
Game over.
And what happens next?
The player can restart.
These questions come before the code.
If you can't answer them, you're not ready to build yet. And that's okay. It just means you keep thinking.
Every product can be split into three simple questions.
What exists?
What does it look like?
And what does it do?
On the web, each question has its own language.
HTML creates the things that exist.
CSS decides what they look like.
And JavaScript decides what they do.
Think of a house.
HTML is the walls.
CSS is the paint, and the furniture.
JavaScript is the electricity. It makes things happen.
You don't need any code yet. Just remember the three jobs.
Here's another creator habit.
Know what you need before you start.
Characters. Obstacles. A background. Sounds. Fonts. Buttons. Code. Game rules. And ideas.
Resources can come from lots of places.
You might draw them, build them with CSS, write the code yourself, use AI to explore ideas, or find them from a source you're allowed to use.
The important thing isn't where they come from. It's knowing what you need.
Now we have an idea.
We've seen the finished product.
We've planned it.
We've designed it.
We've broken it into parts.
We know what we need.
Now... we're ready to build.
Here's the path we'll follow for the rest of this series.
Idea. Plan. Design. Building blocks. HTML. CSS. JavaScript. Test. And improve.
And notice the loop at the end. Test, improve, and test again. That's how every product gets better.
There's one more tool in a creator's toolbox.
AI.
But notice when we brought it in. After the thinking.
When you have a clear requirement, AI can help explain how to do it.
When you have a problem, AI can help you investigate it.
When you have an idea, AI can help you think it through.
Now notice what we didn't say.
Make me a game.
Instead, we ask. Understand. Test. Check. And improve.
The better you understand your project, the better you can use AI.
AI can help you build faster.
But the idea, the decisions, and the understanding, still belong to you.
Your turn.
Grab some paper, and design your own version.
Draw your player. An obstacle. The game area. The score. A restart button. And what happens when the player hits an obstacle.
Then answer five questions.
What will my game look like? What can the player do? What happens when the player makes a mistake? What do I need to build it? And what could make my version different?
Maybe your player is a cat. Maybe the obstacles are puddles. Maybe it's a robot, running on Mars. It's your design.
Keep your design. We're going to use it.
Next time, we'll take this design, and build its structure, using HTML.
